In this proof we drop the subscript <MATH_0001> from our pullback
and pushforward functors.
Denote <MATH_0002> and denote <MATH_0003> the
morphism <MATH_0004>.
Let <MATH_0005> be a descent datum for <MATH_0006>.
Let us set <MATH_0007>.
We may think of <MATH_0008> as defining an isomorphism
<MATH_0009>.
We claim that the rule which sends a descent datum
<MATH_0010>
to the sheaf
<MATH_0011>
is a quasi-inverse to the functor in the statement of the lemma.
The first of the two arrows comes from the map
<MATH_0012>
and the second arrow comes from the map
<MATH_0013>
where the arrow pointing left is invertible.
To prove this works we have to show
that the canonical map <MATH_0014>
is an isomorphism; details omitted. In order to prove this it
suffices to check after pulling back by any collection of morphisms
<MATH_0015> where <MATH_0016> is an algebraically closed field.
Namely, the corresponding base changes <MATH_0017> are jointly
surjective and we can check whether a map of sheaves on <MATH_0018>
is an isomorphism by looking at stalks on geometric points, see
Theorem <REF_0001>.
By Lemma <REF_0002>
the construction of <MATH_0019> from the descent datum
<MATH_0020> commutes with any base change.
Thus we may assume <MATH_0021> is the spectrum of an algebraically
closed field (note that base change preserves the properties
of the morphism <MATH_0022>, see
Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0003>
and <REF_0004>).
In this case the morphism <MATH_0023> has a section, so we
know that the functor is an equivalence by
Lemma <REF_0005>.
However, the reader may show that the functor is an equivalence
if and only if the construction above is a quasi-inverse;
details omitted. This finishes the proof.
